claim: SNUL-1 RNA forms a distinct territory within the nucleolus in human cell lines.
source: In a screen to identify cell-cycle-regulated RNAs with distinct cellular distribution (Hao et al., 2020), we identified a unique probe with ~600 nucleotides (Supplementary file 1), which hybridized to an RNA species that preferentially formed a cloud/territory within the nucleolus in a broad spectrum of human cell lines (Figure 1A–B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 localization in multiple cell lines, as referenced in the figures.

claim: SNUL-1 RNA decorates only one nucleolus per nucleus in most diploid or near-diploid cells.
source: Unlike other nucleolus-resident RNAs, which are homogeneously distributed in all the nucleoli within a cell, this RNA cloud decorated only one nucleolus (even in cells with several nucleoli) per nucleus in most of the diploid or near-diploid cells (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; embryonic stem cell [WA09], fibroblasts [WI-38, IMR-90, and MCH065], epithelial cell [hTERT-RPE-1], and lymphocyte [GM12878]).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data across multiple diploid cell lines showing single nucleolus localization.

claim: Cancer cell lines display varied numbers of SNUL-1 territories per nucleus ranging from 1 to 4 clouds per cell.
source: Strikingly, cancer cell lines displayed varied numbers of the SNUL-1 territories per nucleus (ranging from 1 to 4 SNUL-1 clouds/cell), lthough the number of SNUL-1 cloud/cell remained fixed for a particular cell line (Figure 1B–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RNA-FISH data from cancer cell lines shown in the figures.

claim: The SNUL-1 cloud is preserved in biochemically isolated nucleoli.
source: The SNUL-1 cloud was well-preserved even in biochemically isolated nucleoli (Figure 1D), indicating that SNUL-1 associates with integral components of the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data on isolated nucleoli showing preserved SNUL-1 distribution.

claim: SNUL-1 associates with integral components of the nucleolus.
source: The SNUL-1 cloud was well-preserved even in biochemically isolated nucleoli (Figure 1D), indicating that SNUL-1 associates with integral components of the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SNUL-1 remains localized after biochemical isolation of nucleoli.

claim: SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 are members of a novel RNA family that form non-overlapping constrained territories within the nucleolus.
source: Based on this, we propose that SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 are members of a novel RNA family and form non-overlapping constrained territories within the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing distinct localization patterns of SNUL-1 and SNUL-2.

claim: SNUL-1 probe contains a [CT]20 repeat and a 60-nucleotide overhang sequence that are crucial for detecting the SNUL-1 cloud.
source: RNA-FISH-based analyses revealed that a [CT]20 repeat and a 60-nucleotide overhang sequence within the original probe-1 were crucial for detecting the SNUL-1 cloud (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D; probe 4), implying that the [AG] repeats along with unique sequence beyond the repeat contributes to the hybridization specificity and localization of SNUL-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RNA-FISH data using truncated probes to identify minimal required sequences.

claim: SNUL-1 represents a group of RNA species that share similar sequence features and are clustered together as an RNA cloud within the nucleolus.
source: Thus, it is plausible that rather than a single type of transcript, SNUL-1 represents a group of RNA species that share similar sequence features and are clustered together as an RNA cloud within the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is supported by PacBio Iso-seq and Nanopore sequencing data showing multiple candidate sequences with high similarity.

claim: SNUL-1 candidate sequences range in length from 1.9 kb to 3.1 kb.
source: The full-length SNUL-1 candidates identified by iso-sequencing ranged in length from 1.9 kb-3.1 kb (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PacBio Iso-seq data showing the size distribution of candidate sequences.

claim: SNUL-1 candidate sequences display high levels of sequence similarity between each other (>90%).
source: The full-length SNUL-1 CS RNAs identified by both iso-seq and nanopore seq. analyses contained defined 5' and 3' ends, and displayed high levels of sequence similarity between each other (>90%) (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data from PacBio and Nanopore sequencing.

claim: SNUL-1 candidate sequences show ~84–91% sequence similarity to 21S pre-rRNA.
source: Pair-wise alignment of the individual members of the SNUL-1 CSs with the transcribed region of rDNA revealed ~84–91% sequence similarity between the CSs and one of the pre-rRNA species, 21 S (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by pairwise sequence alignment data comparing SNUL-1 candidates to 21S pre-rRNA.

claim: 21S pre-rRNA is an intermediate produced during rRNA processing, consisting of 18S and partial ITS1.
source: 21 S is one of the intermediates produced during rRNA processing, consisting of 18 S and partial ITS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of rRNA processing pathways.

claim: SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA distribute in mostly non-overlapping regions within the nucleolus.
source: In the nucleolus, both SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA (detected by the probe hybridizing to the internal transcribed region [ITS1] of pre-rRNA) distributed mostly non-overlapping regions, as observed by super resolution-structured illumination microscopy (SR-SIM) imaging (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging data showing spatial distribution of SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA.

claim: Modified DNA antisense oligonucleotides against SNUL (ASO-SNUL) specifically reduce SNUL-1 levels.
source: In addition, modified DNA antisense oligonucleotides against SNUL (ASO-SNUL) specifically reduced only SNUL-1 levels. (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing loss of SNUL-1 signal after ASO treatment.

claim: SNUL-1 is preferentially enriched in the DFC (dense fibrillar center) sub-nucleolar region.
source: SR-SIM imaging revealed that SNUL-1 distributed across all three sub-nucleolar compartments (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) but was preferentially enriched in the DFC region (higher Pearson's correlation coefficient [PCC] between SNUL-1 and FBL [DFC marker] over RPA194 [FC marker]; Figure 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging and quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficients.

claim: SNUL-1 is associated with transcriptionally active DFC/FC units as shown by 5-FU incorporation.
source: The SNUL-1 cloud is also associated with the transcriptionally active DFC/FC units, as observed by the presence of 5-FU (fluro-uridine)-incorporated nascent RNA in SNUL-1-associated domains (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by 5-FU metabolic labeling experiments showing nascent RNA synthesis in SNUL-1 regions.

claim: SNUL-1 and nascent pre-rRNA co-exist within the same FC/DFC unit but are not colocalized.
source: However, the SNUL-1 and nascent pre-rRNA were not colocalized but co-existed within the same FC/DFC unit, as observed and quantified by SR-SIM imaging and PCC analyses (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging and Pearson's correlation coefficient analysis.

claim: SNUL-1 co-occupies with pre-rRNA in approximately 4 adjacent FC/DFC units within a single nucleolus.
source: SNUL-1 co-occupied with pre-rRNA in ~4 adjacent FC/DFC units within a single nucleolus (Figure 2G) (n=22).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of SR-SIM imaging data from 22 nucleoli.

claim: SNUL-1 is transcribed by RNA Polymerase I.
source: SNUL-1 is transcribed by RNA Pol I, as cells treated with RNA Pol I inhibitors (BMH21 or low dose of Actinomycin D [ActD, 10 ng/ml]) showed reduced SNUL-1 levels (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing reduced SNUL-1 levels after treatment with RNA Pol I inhibitors.

claim: SNUL-1 levels are not significantly affected by RNA Polymerase II inhibition.
source: On the other hand, the level of SNUL-1 was not significantly affected by RNA Polymerase II inhibition with drugs, including CDK9 inhibitors flavopiridol and 5,6-Dichloro-1-β-d-ribofuranosylbenzimidazole (DRB; Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing maintained SNUL-1 levels after RNA Pol II inhibitor treatment.

claim: Upon RNA Pol II inhibition, SNUL-1 is moved and preserved at the nucleolar periphery decorated by pre-rRNA.
source: However, upon RNA Pol II inhibition SNUL-1 were moved and preserved at the nucleolar periphery decorated by pre-rRNA (Boulon et al., 2010; Haaf and Ward, 1996; Figure 2I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F; please see figure inset), and this alteration in the RNA distribution was reversible during transcription re-activation (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 relocalization after DRB treatment and recovery experiments, with citations to previous studies.

claim: The SNUL-1 cloud is absent from pro-metaphase to anaphase during mitosis.
source: The SNUL-1 cloud was absent from pro-metaphase to anaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing absence of SNUL-1 signal during specific mitotic phases.

claim: In telophase/early G1 nuclei, a prominent single SNUL-1 cloud co-localizes with one of the several rRNA-containing active NORs.
source: In the telophase/early G1 nuclei in multiple cell lines, we observed a prominent single SNUL-1 cloud co-localized with one of the several rRNAs containing active NORs (see arrow in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from telophase/early G1 cells showing SNUL-1 localization with NORs.

claim: Late telophase or early G1 cells show a weak but distinct second SNUL-1 signal associating with another active NOR.
source: Late telophase or early G1 cells also showed a weak but distinct second SNUL-1 signal associating with another active NOR (please see arrowhead in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing a second weaker SNUL-1 signal in early G1 cells.

claim: In interphase nuclei, only one SNUL-1 cloud is observed that is specifically associated with a single NOR-containing chromosome allele.
source: In the interphase nuclei, only one SNUL-1 cloud was observed that was specifically associated with a single NOR-containing chromosome allele (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 association with a single NOR-containing chromosome.

claim: In WI-38 interphase nuclei, the SNUL-1 cloud is specifically associated (100% association) with one allele of Chr. 15.
source: Further experiments revealed that in WI-38 interphase nuclei, including in G1 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is specifically associated (100% association) with one allele of Chr. 15 (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-RNA and DNA-FISH data showing complete association of SNUL-1 with one Chr. 15 allele.

claim: The association rate between the SNUL-1 cloud and other NOR-containing chromosomes such as Chr. 13 and Chr. 22 is 30–40%.
source: The association rate between the SNUL-1 cloud and other NOR-containing chromosomes, such as Chr. 13 and Chr. 22 was 30–40%, which could be because these chromosomes are localized in the same nucleolus, along with the SNUL-1-associated Chr. 15 allele.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative DNA-RNA-FISH data and includes an inference about spatial proximity.

claim: Monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 is confirmed in several human cell lines including primary fibroblasts, hTERT-RPE1, and HTD114 cells.
source: Monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 was also confirmed in several other human cell lines, including in primary fibroblasts (IMR-90 [lung], MCH065 [dermal]), hTERT-immortalized near-diploid retinal pigment epithelial cells (hTERT-RPE1) and Fibrosarcoma (HTD114) cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D; Figure 4C; Breger et al., 2004; Gupta et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data from multiple cell lines with citations to cell line sources.

claim: SNUL-2 RNA cloud is specifically associated with one allele of the NOR-containing Chr. 13.
source: Like SNUL-1, SNUL-2 RNA cloud is specifically associated with one allele of the NOR-containing Chr.13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-2 association with Chr. 13.

claim: A unique subset of SNUL-like genes may be present in each of the five NOR-containing acrocentric chromosome arms.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that a unique subset of SNUL-like genes may be present in each of the five NOR-containing acrocentric chromosome arms, where each member of the SNUL RNA (SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 on Chr.15 and 13, respectively) form spatially constrained RNA territories on the p-arm of the chromosome alleles.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation of SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 association with different chromosomes.

claim: SNUL-1 is transcribed from Chr. 15 by RNA pol I and forms a confined RNA territory in the nucleolus.
source: By utilizing the mouse A9 cells integrated with one allele of human Chr. 15 (mono-chromosomal somatic cell hybrid A9 +H15) (van Sluis et al., 2019), we further confirmed that SNUL-1 is indeed transcribed from Chr. 15 by RNA pol I and formed a confined RNA territory in the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using somatic cell hybrids with citation to the cell line source.

claim: Exogenous expression of human TBP-associated factors (TAF1A-D) in A9+H15 cells reactivates RNA Pol I transcription from human Chr. 15.
source: Exogenous expression of human TBP-associated factors (TAF1A-D) in the A9 +H15 cells reactivated RNA Pol I transcription from human Chr. 15, reflected by the presence of both human rRNA and SNUL-1 in the nucleolus (Figure 3D; van Sluis et al., 2019; Murano et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from transfection experiments with citations to previous studies.

claim: WI-38 cells have equal rDNA content between the two Chr. 15 alleles.
source: Quantification of the integrated density of the rDNA spots on the mitotic chromosome spreads of WI-38 confirmed equal rDNA content between the two Chr.15 alleles (Figure 3E–F; green).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative DNA-FISH data on metaphase chromosomes.

claim: The monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 in WI-38 cells is not dictated by the rDNA content.
source: This indicates that the monoallelic association of SNUL-1 to Chr. 15 in WI-38 cells is not dictated by the rDNA content in these cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of equal rDNA content between Chr. 15 alleles despite monoallelic SNUL-1 association.

claim: SNUL-1-decorated Chr. 15 allele contains transcriptionally active rDNA clusters as shown by positive 5-FU incorporation.
source: We further observed that SNUL-1-decorated Chr. 15 allele contained transcriptionally active rDNA clusters as shown by positive 5-FU incorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by 5-FU metabolic labeling experiments showing active transcription.

claim: UBF is present in both Chr. 15 alleles, implying that SNUL-1-decorated NORs contain transcriptionally active rDNA clusters.
source: Previous studies have established RNA pol I transcription factor, UBF as a marker for transcriptionally active NORs (McStay, 2023; van Sluis et al., 2020; van Sluis et al., 2016). We observed the presence of UBF in both the Chr. 15 alleles, implying that SNUL-1-decorated NORs contain transcriptionally active rDNA clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing UBF localization, with citations to previous studies establishing UBF as an active NOR marker.

claim: WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1 cells show a significant difference in the size of the Chr. 15-specific peri-centromeric Sat III repeat signal between the two Chr. 15 alleles.
source: We consistently observed a significant difference in the size of the Chr. 15-specific peri-centromeric Sat III repeat (15Sat III) signal between the two Chr. 15 alleles in several of the diploid or pseudo-diploid cell lines ([WI-38; Figure 3E; Figure 4A–B], [hTERT-RPE-1; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G & Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B], [MCH065; Figure 4C]), implying that these cells showed allele-specific differences in the amount or compaction of peri-centromeric 15Sat III DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-FISH data showing differential 15Sat III signal intensity between alleles.

claim: In 100% of WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is associated only with the larger 15Sat III signal containing Chr. 15 allele.
source: Interestingly, in 100% of WI-38 and hTERT-RPE1 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud was associated only with the larger 15Sat III signal containing Chr.15 allele (Figure 4A–B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B; n=50 from biological triplicates).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative DNA-RNA-FISH data from 50 cells across biological triplicates.

claim: In MCH065 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is associated with the Chr. 15 allele containing the smaller 15Sat III signal.
source: On the other hand, the SNUL-1 cloud in the MCH065 cells was associated with the Chr. 15 allele containing the smaller 15Sat III signal (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data from MCH065 cells.

claim: SNUL-1 is either imprinted or displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association in a cell type-specific manner.
source: These results suggest that SNUL-1 is either imprinted or display mitotically inherited random monoallelic association in a cell type-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of cell line-specific differences in SNUL-1 association with different Chr. 15 alleles.

claim: SNULs do not influence allele-specific 15Sat III levels or compaction.
source: Loss-of-function studies revealed that SNULs did not influence allele-specific 15Sat III levels or compaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-FISH data from SNUL-depleted cells showing no change in 15Sat III signal.

claim: In WI-38 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is preferentially located away from the paternal Chr. 15 allele co-expressing SNRPN and SPA2.
source: In WI-38 cells (n=75), the SNUL-1 cloud was preferentially located away from the paternal Chr.15 allele, co-expressing SNRPN and SPA2 (Figure 4E–F), indicating that in WI-38 cells, SNUL-1 associated with the maternal allele of Chr. 15, which also contains larger 15SatIII.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing spatial separation of SNUL-1 from paternally expressed genes.

claim: In WI-38 cells, SNUL-1 associates with the maternal allele of Chr. 15.
source: In WI-38 cells (n=75), the SNUL-1 cloud was preferentially located away from the paternal Chr.15 allele, co-expressing SNRPN and SPA2 (Figure 4E–F), indicating that in WI-38 cells, SNUL-1 associated with the maternal allele of Chr. 15, which also contains larger 15SatIII.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SNUL-1 is located away from paternally expressed genes.

claim: In MCH065 fibroblasts, MCH065-derived iPSCs (MCH2-10), and HTD114 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud is associated with the paternal Chr. 15 allele.
source: On the other hand, in the MCH065 Fibroblasts, MCH065-derived iPSCs (MCH2-10), and HTD114 cells, the SNUL-1 cloud was associated with the paternal Chr. 15 allele, as demonstrated by the localization of SNUL-1 cloud next to the smaller 15SatIII or SNRPN RNA signals (Figure 4C–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL-1 association with the paternal allele in multiple cell lines.

claim: SNUL-1 is not an imprinted gene but rather displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association (rMA) to paternal or maternal Chr. 15 in a cell line-specific manner.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that SNUL-1 is not an imprinted gene but rather displays mitotically inherited random monoallelic association (rMA) to paternal or maternal Chr. 15 in a cell line-specific manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M; Reinius and Sandberg, 2015; Chess, 2016).
evidence: The claim is concluded from data showing variable parental allele association across cell lines, with citations to previous studies on monoallelic expression.

claim: WI-38 cells co-incubated with 5-Aza-dC and TSA show two separate SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 foci.
source: WI-38 cells co-incubated with 5-Aza-2'-deoxycytidine (5-Aza-dC), which inhibits DNA methyl transferase (DNMT) and Trichostatin A (TSA), which inhibits histone deacetylase (HDAC) showed two separate SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 foci (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from cells treated with epigenetic modifier inhibitors.

claim: Both SNUL-1 clouds in 5-Aza-dC+TSA-treated cells remain localized in the nucleolus and are associated with both Chr. 15 alleles in a population of cells.
source: Both the SNUL-1 clouds in 5-Aza-dC+TSA-treated cells remained localized in the nucleolus (Figure 4I) and were associated with both Chr. 15 alleles in a population of cells (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH and DNA-RNA-FISH data from treated cells.

claim: Repressive epigenetic regulators are potentially involved in maintaining the monoallelic association of SNULs.
source: These results indicate the potential involvement of repressive epigenetic regulators in maintaining the monoallelic association of SNULs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that inhibiting DNA methylation and histone deacetylation leads to biallelic SNUL expression.

claim: Modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting individual SNUL-1 CS candidates did not reduce total SNUL-1 levels.
source: Modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs; ASO112 and ASO113) targeting individual SNUL-1 CS candidates did not reduce total SNUL-1 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing maintained SNUL-1 signal after treatment with specific ASOs.

claim: ASO-SNUL targeting the repeat sequence within SNULs efficiently depletes both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2.
source: The repeat sequence within SNULs was highly conserved among all the SNUL-1 CSs and was also shared by the SNUL-2 transcript. Using an ASO targeting this region (ASO-SNUL), we efficiently depleted both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data showing loss of both SNUL-1 and SNUL-2 signals after ASO-SNUL treatment.

claim: SNUL-depleted WI-38 cells show enhanced 5-FU incorporation in the nucleolus.
source: Interestingly, SNUL-depleted WI-38 showed enhanced 5-FU incorporation in the nucleolus (Figure 5B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by 5-FU metabolic labeling data showing increased signal in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: SNUL-depleted cells show increased levels of nascent 47S pre-rRNA.
source: and showed increased levels of nascent 47 S pre-rRNA, quantified by single molecule RNA-Fluorescent hybridization (smRNA-FISH) using a probe set (5'ETS-2) that preferentially detects nascent 47 S pre-rRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by smRNA-FISH data showing increased pre-rRNA signal in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: A similar increase in pre-rRNA levels is observed upon SNUL depletion in RPE-1 and HTD114 cell lines.
source: A similar increase in the pre-rRNA levels was also observed upon SNUL depletion in other cell lines, including RPE-1 (SNUL-1 associates with the maternal Chr.15 allele) and HTD114 (SNUL-1 associates with the paternal Chr.15 allele; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-FISH data from multiple cell lines showing increased pre-rRNA after SNUL depletion.

claim: RNA FISH-FLOW assay shows increased pre-rRNA levels in RPE1 cells upon SNUL depletion.
source: In addition, we quantified the pre-rRNA levels in a population of RPE1 cells using the recently developed RNA FISH-FLOW (Antony et al., 2022) assay and observed a similar increase in pre-rRNA levels upon SNUL depletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA FISH-FLOW data with citation to the method.

claim: SNUL depletion either enhances the expression of nucleolus-enriched rRNA genes and/or alters the co-transcriptional pre-rRNA processing.
source: Our results imply that SNUL depletion either enhanced the expression of nucleolus-enriched rRNA genes and/or altered the co-transcriptional pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of increased pre-rRNA levels in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: SNUL-depleted cells show an increased number of FC/DFC compartments per nucleolus.
source: We observed that SNUL-depleted cells showed an increased number of FC/DFC compartments/nucleolus (Figure 5D and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) by performing SIM imaging of nucleolar proteins decorating specific sub-nucleolar compartments.
evidence: The claim is supported by SIM imaging data showing increased FC/DFC units in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: SNUL-depleted cells show smaller fibrillarin-stained DFC rings and larger RPA194 decorated FC domains.
source: SNUL-depleted cells specifically showed smaller fibrillarin-stained DFC rings and larger RPA194 decorated FC domains, as observed in averaged images of FC and DFC domains using Average Intensity Projections (n=20; Figure 5G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative SIM imaging analysis of FC and DFC domain sizes.

claim: The changes in the number and size of FC/DFC domains in SNUL-depleted cells could be a consequence of altered pre-rRNA expression.
source: The changes in the number and size of FC/DFC domains in SNUL-depleted cells could be a consequence of altered pre-rRNA expression in these cells.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the relationship between altered pre-rRNA expression and nucleolar organization changes.

claim: The nascent 47S pre-rRNA is co-transcriptionally sorted from its transcription site at the DFC/FC boundary to DFC.
source: The nascent 47 S pre-rRNA is co-transcriptionally sorted from its transcription site at the DFC/FC boundary to DFC (Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claim: DFC-localized FBL binds to the 5' end upstream of the first cleavage site (01 site) of the 47S pre-rRNA co-transcriptionally.
source: The DFC-localized FBL binds to the 5' end upstream of the first cleavage site (01 site; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; Figure 5I) of the 47 S pre-rRNA co-transcriptionally and facilitates pre-rRNA sorting for efficient RNA processing and DFC assembly (Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claim: In SNUL-depleted cells, the FBL-interacting 5'ETS-1 region within the 47S pre-rRNA fails to sort to DFC and instead preferentially accumulates in the FC.
source: Interestingly, in the SNUL-depleted cells, the FBL-interacting 5'ETS-1 region within the 47 S pre-rRNA failed to sort to DFC and instead preferentially accumulated in the FC (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SIM imaging data showing altered localization of 5'ETS-1 signal in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of pre-rRNA processing factors such as FBL compromises 47S pre-rRNA sorting at DFC, resulting in accumulation of pre-rRNA in the FC region.
source: An earlier study demonstrated that depletion of pre-rRNA processing factors, such as FBL, compromised 47 S pre-rRNA sorting at DFC, resulting in the accumulation of pre-rRNA in the FC region (Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claim: SNULs could influence pre-rRNA biogenesis by modulating FBL-mediated pre-rRNA sorting/processing.
source: Our results suggest the possibility that SNULs could influence pre-rRNA biogenesis by modulating FBL-mediated pre-rRNA sorting/processing.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation of altered pre-rRNA sorting in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: SNUL-depleted cells show reduced interaction between FBL and pre-rRNA.
source: Strikingly, SNUL-depleted cells showed reduced interaction between FBL and pre-rRNA (Figure 5J), indicating that DFC-enriched SNULs could influence the FBL interaction with pre-rRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by FBL RNA-immunoprecipitation followed by quantitative RT-PCR data.

claim: DFC-enriched SNULs could influence the FBL interaction with pre-rRNA.
source: Strikingly, SNUL-depleted cells showed reduced interaction between FBL and pre-rRNA (Figure 5J), indicating that DFC-enriched SNULs could influence the FBL interaction with pre-rRNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of reduced FBL-pre-rRNA interaction in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: SNUL-1-depleted cells show defects in the initial cleavage at the 5' end of the 47S pre-rRNA.
source: SNUL-1-depleted cells showed defects in the initial cleavage at the 5'end of the 47 S pre-rRNA, as observed by the reduced levels of 30S+1 intermediate and +1–01 cleaved product (Figure 5K; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D) by Northern blot analyses.
evidence: The claim is supported by Northern blot data showing altered pre-rRNA processing intermediates.

claim: SNULs are potentially involved in pre-rRNA sorting and/or co-transcriptional processing.
source: These results indicate the potential involvement of SNULs in pre-rRNA, sorting and/or co-transcriptional processing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple observations including altered pre-rRNA sorting, FBL interaction, and processing defects in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: NcRNAs influence asynchronous DNA replication in a monoallelic fashion.
source: NcRNAs influence asynchronous DNA replication in a monoallelic fashion.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ncRNA functions.

claim: ASARs are monoallelically transcribed lncRNAs that control asynchronous replication timing between chromosome alleles.
source: For example, Thayer laboratory has identified a group of lncRNAs, ASARs (Asynchronous replication and Autosomal RNAs), which are monoallelically transcribed and associated on various chromosomes and control asynchronous replication timing between chromosome alleles (Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Donley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: An earlier study reported allelic-specific replication and transcription of rDNA loci in human cells.
source: An earlier study from Cedar laboratory reported allelic-specific replication and transcription of rDNA loci in human cells (Schlesinger et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claim: In control HTD114 and WI-38 cells, both alleles of Chr. 15 p-arms replicate during the late S phase.
source: In contrary to what had been reported by the Cedar group, we did not observe allele-specific differential replication of rDNA clusters on the Chr.15 p-arm. Both the alleles of Chr.15 p-arms replicate during the late S phase in both the cell lines (please see Ctrl in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ReTiSH assay data showing synchronous replication of both Chr. 15 alleles.

claim: Upon SNUL-depletion in HTD114 cells, the maternal allele of Chr. 15 p-arm replicates earlier compared to the paternal allele.
source: Surprisingly, upon SNUL-depletion, the Chr. 15 alleles showed differential replication timing. In SNUL-depleted HTD114 cells, the maternal allele of Chr.15 p-arm (allele with larger CEN15 signal) replicated earlier (no rDNA signal in 6 hr) compared to the paternal allele, which continued to replicate during late S-phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,C; compare 6 hr Ctrl versus 6 hr ASO-SNUL).
evidence: The claim is supported by ReTiSH assay data comparing control and SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: EdU-incorporation assays confirm that upon SNUL depletion, the replication timing of the maternal Chr. 15 allele shifts from late S-phase to middle S-phase.
source: To independently test the ReTiSH results, we performed EdU-incorporation assays in control and SNUL-depleted interphase HTD114 cells. Cells were pulse-labelled with EdU to mark replication sites (green), co-stained with rDNA (Cyan) and Chr.15-specific centromeres (yellow) to determine the replication timing of the Chr.15 p-arm containing rDNA cluster (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C). In control cells, rDNA cluster from both the chr-15 p-arms co-localized with EdU +ve foci predominantly in mid and late S-phase cells. Upon SNUL depletion, Chr. 15 rDNA cluster from the maternal allele showed enhanced association with EdU foci in the middle S-phase cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A–C). These results implicate that the replication timing of maternal allele shifts from late S-phase to middle S-phase upon SNUL depletion, confirming the ReTiSH results.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation assay data confirming the ReTiSH findings.

claim: Active histone marks (H3Ac, H4Ac, H3K4me3) are not differentially distributed between the two Chr. 15 p-arm alleles in control and SNUL-depleted HTD114 and RPE1 cells.
source: However, unlike what had been reported earlier by the Cedar lab in their earlier study, we could not find any active histone marks in both the alleles of rDNA bearing p-arms of Chr. 15 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6; Figure 5—figure supplement 7) in control as well as SNUL-depleted cells. We measured the histone mark signal intensities between two chr. 15 p-arm alleles and did not find any significant difference between the two alleles in control and SNUL-depleted cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data on metaphase spreads showing no differential histone marks.

claim: Monoallelic replication and transcription of Chr. 15 rDNA cluster containing NORs is not observed in human cell lines (hTERT-RPE1, HTD114, and WI-38) that display monoallelic association of SNULs.
source: In conclusion, we did not find monoallelic replication and transcription of chr. 15 rDNA cluster containing NORs in human cell lines (hTERT-RPE1, HTD114, and WI-38) those display monoallelic association of SNULs, supporting the notion that every NORs contain both active and inactive rDNA clusters.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the replication timing and histone mark data showing no monoallelic differences.

claim: SNUL RNAs constitute the first family of ncRNAs in the nucleolus that displays monoallelic association to specific NOR-containing chromosomes.
source: Based on these results, we argue that SNUL RNAs constitute the first family of ncRNAs in the nucleolus, which displays monollelic association to specific NOR-containing chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the collective data showing monoallelic SNUL association without monoallelic rDNA replication or transcription.

claim: SNUL-1 is a member of a family of RNAs sharing similar sequence features.
source: We have discovered SNULs, a novel family of ncRNAs, which display non-random association to specific NOR-containing chromosomes within the nucleolus. Our data suggest that SNUL-1 is a member of a family of RNAs sharing similar sequence features.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data showing multiple SNUL-1 candidate sequences with high similarity.

claim: The most striking feature of the SNUL-1 sequence is its resemblance to the 21S pre-rRNA intermediate.
source: The most striking feature of the SNUL-1 sequence is its resemblance to the 21 S pre-rRNA intermediate.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data showing high similarity between SNUL-1 and 21S pre-rRNA.

claim: Most sequences in the NOR-containing p-arms are shared among all 5 acrocentric chromosomes.
source: Recent genomic mapping of acrocentric chromosome arms revealed that most of the sequences in the NOR-containing p-arms are shared among all 5 chromosomes (Floutsakou et al., 2013; van Sluis et al., 2019; Nurk et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous genomic studies.

claim: Genomic studies have identified inter-chromosomal sequence variations in acrocentric chromosome p-arms.
source: However, these studies have also identified inter-chromosomal sequence variations (van Sluis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claim: The association of individual members of SNULs to specific alleles of acrocentric chromosomes supports the idea that acrocentric arms encode chromosome- and allele-specific transcripts.
source: Our observations showing the association of individual members of SNULs to specific alleles of one of the acrocentric chromosomes support the idea that the acrocentric arms encode chromosome- and allele-specific transcripts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of chromosome-specific SNUL association patterns.

claim: The underlying mechanism(s) controlling differential expression of rRNA gene copies in mammals is yet to be determined.
source: The underlying mechanism(s) controlling differential expression of rRNA gene copies in mammals is yet to be determined.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about gaps in understanding rRNA gene regulation.

claim: Nucleolar dominance (NuD) is a developmentally regulated process speculated to act as a dosage-control system to adjust the number of actively transcribed rRNA genes.
source: Nucleolar dominance (NuD) is a developmentally regulated process that is speculated to act as a dosage-control system to adjust the number of actively transcribed rRNA genes according to the cellular need (McStay and Grummt, 2008; Grummt and Pikaard, 2003).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: NuD is primarily observed in interspecies hybrids of plants, invertebrates, amphibians, and mammals.
source: However, NuD is primarily observed in the 'interspecies hybrids' of plants, invertebrates, amphibians, and mammals (Tucker et al., 2010; McStay, 2006; Cassidy and Blackler, 1974; Goodrich-Young and Krider, 1989; Croce et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: NuD is reported in certain nonhybrid or 'pure species' of plants and fruit flies but has not yet been observed in mammals.
source: NuD is reported in certain nonhybrid or 'pure species' of plants and fruit flies but has not yet been observed in mammals, primarily due to a lack of information about the allele-specific rRNA sequence variations (Lewis et al., 2004; Greil and Ahmad, 2012; Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: During NuD, the rRNA gene array from one parent (dominant) is maintained transcriptionally active while the rRNA loci from the other parent (under dominant) are preferentially silenced.
source: During NuD, chromosome allele-specific rRNA expression is observed, in which the rRNA gene array within the NOR that is inherited from one parent (dominant) is maintained in a transcriptionally active status, while the rRNA loci from the other parent (under dominant) are preferentially silenced (McStay, 2006; Pontes et al., 2007; Earley et al., 2010; Chen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: Several features associated with the monoallelic regulation of SNULs share similarities with NuD.
source: Several features associated with the monoallelic regulation of SNULs share similarities with NuD (Tucker et al., 2010; McStay, 2006).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing SNUL regulation features with known NuD characteristics, with citations to NuD studies.

claim: SNUL-1 and rRNA expression in NuD is dictated by non-imprinted random monoallelic expression.
source: SNUL-1 and rRNA expression in NuD is dictated by non-imprinted random monoallelic expression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SNUL-1 shows random monoallelic association similar to NuD patterns.

claim: Repressive epigenetic modifiers play vital roles in the allele-specific expression of SNULs and rRNAs during NuD.
source: Repressive epigenetic modifiers play vital roles in the allele-specific expression of SNULs, and rRNAs during NuD (Earley et al., 2010; Chen and Pikaard, 1997; Neves et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing biallelic SNUL expression after epigenetic modifier inhibition, with citations to NuD studies.

claim: Specific sequence elements located near the NORs are implicated in controlling NuD.
source: Interestingly, specific sequence elements located near the NORs are implicated in controlling NuD (Labhart and Reeder, 1984; Rabanal et al., 2017; Warsinger-Pepe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: In germ cells of male Drosophila, Y chromosome sequence elements promote developmentally regulated NuD of Y chromosome-encoded rRNA over X-chromosome rRNA.
source: For example, in the germ cells of male Drosophila, Y chromosome sequence elements promote developmentally regulated NuD of the Y chromosome-encoded rRNA over the X-chromosome rRNA (Warsinger-Pepe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claim: SNUL-1 forms a spatially constrained RNA territory that associates next to the NOR of Chr. 15 but is devoid of pre-rRNA.
source: We observe that SNUL-1 forms a spatially constrained RNA territory that associates next to the NOR of Chr. 15 but is devoid of pre-rRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by SR-SIM imaging data showing spatial separation of SNUL-1 and pre-rRNA.

claim: SNUL-depleted cells show elevated levels of pre-rRNA along with defects in pre-rRNA sorting and processing.
source: Furthermore, SNUL-depleted cells show elevated levels of pre-rRNA, along with defects in pre-rRNA sorting and processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data including RNA-FISH, SIM imaging, and Northern blot analyses.

claim: SNUL-1 could modulate rRNA expression by competing for and/or recruiting factors that regulate rRNA biogenesis in a spatially constrained area within the nucleolus.
source: One-way SNUL-1 could modulate rRNA expression is via modulating the levels of bioprocessing machinery that control rRNA biogenesis and processing. For example, high sequence similarity between SNUL-1 and pre-rRNAs helps SNUL-1 to compete for and/or recruit factors that regulate rRNA biogenesis in a spatially constrained area within the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism by which SNUL-1 might regulate rRNA expression.

claim: Pre-rRNAs transcribed from individual NORs form constrained territories that are tethered to the NOR-containing chromosomal regions.
source: A recent study, by visualizing the distribution of tagged pre-rRNAs from an NOR-containing chromosome, reported that similar to SNULs, pre-rRNAs transcribed from individual NORs form constrained territories that are tethered to the NOR-containing chromosomal regions (Mangan and McStay, 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claim: SNUL-1, by forming a distinct RNA territory on the NOR of the Chr. 15 allele, may influence the expression of rRNA genes in cis.
source: It is possible that SNUL-1, by forming a distinct RNA territory on the NOR of the Chr. 15 allele, influences the expression of rRNA genes in cis.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about how SNUL-1 territorial organization might affect rRNA gene expression.

claim: The organization of SNULs and rRNA territories in a constrained area within the nucleolus would help control the expression of a subset of rRNA genes without affecting the rRNA territories on other acrocentric chromosomes.
source: Such organization of SNULs and rRNA territories in a constrained area within the nucleolus would help to control the expression of a subset of rRNA genes without affecting the rRNA territories on other acrocentric chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the functional significance of compartmentalized SNUL and rRNA organization.

claim: The compartmentalized distribution of individual members of SNUL RNA within specific sub-nucleolar regions challenges the current view that all nucleoli within a single nucleus are composed of identical domains.
source: Our observation of the compartmentalized distribution of individual members of SNUL RNA within specific sub-nucleolar regions challenges the current view that all the nucleoli within a single nucleus are composed of identical domains.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of distinct SNUL territories in different nucleoli.

claim: Very little is known about the sequences in the short arms of NOR-containing chromosomes.
source: Presently, very little is known about the sequences in the short arms of NOR-containing chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the state of genomic annotation.

claim: P-arms of NOR-containing chromosomes are enriched with repeat sequences.
source: A recent study utilizing long-read sequencing in a haploid cell line revealed that p-arms of NOR-containing chromosomes are enriched with repeat sequences (Nurk et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a cited previous study.

claim: Higher levels of sequence similarity between SNUL-1 candidates and pre-rRNA made it impossible to precisely map the genomic coordinates of SNUL-1 genes from available long-read sequencing data.
source: Higher levels of sequence similarity observed between SNUL-1 candidates, and pre-rRNA made it impossible for us to precisely map the genomic coordinates of SNUL-1 genes from the available long-read sequencing data set.
evidence: The claim is a statement about technical limitations in mapping SNUL-1 genes.

claim: SNUL-1 candidates show the highest levels of sequence similarity with 21S pre-rRNAs.
source: It is intriguing to note that the SNUL-1 candidates showed the highest levels of sequence similarity with 21 S pre-rRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Many adenosine and guanosine sequence mismatches were observed between SNUL-1 candidates and 21S pre-rRNA.
source: Interestingly, many 'adenosine and Guanosine' sequence mismatches were observed between SNUL-1 candidates and 21 S pre-rRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: SNUL-1 RNAs may represent pre-rRNA variants that are extensively modified via post-transcriptional processes such as adenosine-to-inosine editing.
source: We cannot rule out the possibility that SNUL-1 RNAs represent pre-rRNA variants that are extensively modified via post-transcriptional processes such as adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I-editing).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential origin of SNUL-1 RNAs.

claim: A-to-I editing enzymes such as ADARs are enriched in the nucleolus.
source: Earlier studies have reported the enrichment of A-to-I editing enzymes such as ADARs (Adenosine deaminase that acts on RNA) in the nucleolus and RNA hyper-editing is utilized as a mechanism of RNA nuclear-retention (Sansam et al., 2003; Prasanth et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2008; Zhang and Carmichael, 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: RNA hyper-editing is utilized as a mechanism of RNA nuclear retention.
source: Earlier studies have reported the enrichment of A-to-I editing enzymes such as ADARs (Adenosine deaminase that acts on RNA) in the nucleolus and RNA hyper-editing is utilized as a mechanism of RNA nuclear-retention (Sansam et al., 2003; Prasanth et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2008; Zhang and Carmichael, 2001).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: Complete genome assembly of p-arms from SNUL-1-expressing diploid cells would be essential to map SNUL-1 genes in the genome and identify regulatory elements controlling monoallelic expression of SNULs.
source: Complete genome assembly of p-arms from SNUL-1-expressing diploid cells would be essential to map SNUL-1 genes in the genome and to identify the regulatory elements controlling the monoallelic expression of SNULs.
evidence: The claim is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Genomic annotation of full-length SNUL-1 genes is crucial for designing strategies to specifically alter the expression of individual SNUL genes without targeting other SNUL-like genes.
source: Genomic annotation of the full-length SNUL-1 genes are also crucial for designing strategies to specifically alter the expression of individual SNUL genes without targeting other SNUL-like genes, furthering mechanistic understanding of SNUL functions.
evidence: The claim is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The association of autosome arms by SNULs supports a paradigm-shifting model that ncRNA-coating of chromosomes and their roles in gene repression is not restricted only to sex chromosomes.
source: Even with these technical limitations, the current study is highly impactful because our observations of the association of autosome arms by SNULs support a paradigm-shifting model that ncRNA-coating of chromosomes and their roles in gene repression is not restricted only to sex chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of SNUL association with autosomal chromosomes.

claim: This study will serve as a starting point towards understanding how differential rDNA expression is achieved during physiological processes.
source: In addition, our study will serve as a starting point towards understanding how differential rDNA expression is achieved during physiological processes.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the broader significance of the study.

claim: This study will form the basis for understanding the role of ncRNAs on monoallelic changes in autosomal chromatin structure and gene expression in the nucleolus.
source: Altogether, this study will form the basis for an entirely new avenue of investigation, which would help to understand the role of ncRNAs on monoallelic changes in autosomal chromatin structure and gene expression in the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the broader significance and future impact of the study.

claim: Human cells contain >400 copies of rRNA (18S/28S/5.8S) genes.
source: Human cells contain >400 copies of rRNA (18 S/28 S/5.8 S) genes, yet only ~50% of the copies are transcriptionally active (Grummt, 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claim: Only ~50% of rRNA gene copies are transcriptionally active in human cells.
source: Human cells contain >400 copies of rRNA (18 S/28 S/5.8 S) genes, yet only ~50% of the copies are transcriptionally active (Grummt, 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from a cited previous study.

claim: The expression of rRNA genes is tightly controlled during physiological processes such as cellular development by epigenetic mechanisms.
source: The expression of rRNA genes is tightly controlled during physiological processes, such as cellular development, by epigenetic mechanisms (McStay, 2016; Guetg and Santoro, 2012; McStay and Grummt, 2008; Haaf et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: The mechanism that precisely maintains the dosage of active versus inactive rRNA genes within a cell is yet to be determined.
source: However, the mechanism that precisely maintains the dosage of active versus inactive rRNA genes within a cell is yet to be determined.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about gaps in understanding rRNA gene regulation.

claim: In one scenario, rDNA repeats in half of the 10 NORs remain transcriptionally active while rRNA genes in the rest of the five NORs remain inactive.
source: Two potential scenarios could explain the expression of ~50% rRNA genes at any given time. In the first scenario, rDNA repeats in half of the 10 NORs remain transcriptionally active, whereas the rRNA genes in the rest of the five NORs remain inactive (McStay, 2023; Schlesinger et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis from cited previous studies.

claim: rRNA repeats in individual alleles of Chr. 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 replicate late during the cell cycle and have chromatin marks consistent with being transcriptionally inactive.
source: Supporting this model, a study from Cedar laboratory reported that rRNA repeats present in the NORs of the individual alleles of Chr. 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 replicated late during the cell cycle, and had chromatin marks consistent with transcriptionally being transcriptionally inactive.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a previous study (Cedar laboratory).

claim: In a second scenario, each NOR contains both active and inactive rRNA clusters.
source: In the second scenario, each NOR contains both active and inactive rRNA clusters.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about rRNA gene organization.

claim: All NORs with detectable rDNA repeats are active as defined by UBF loading and their ability to form functional nucleolus.
source: In support of this claim, immune-FISH performed in several non-transformed human cell lines revealed that all the NORs with detectable rDNA repeats are active, as defined by UBF loading and their ability to form functional nucleolus (McStay, 2023; van Sluis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: Recent long-read sequencing data support the hypothesis that each NOR is a mosaic of active rDNA repeat and silent rDNA repeat clusters.
source: Also, recent long-read sequencing data support the hypothesis that each NOR is a mosaic of active rDNA repeat and silent rDNA repeat clusters (van Sluis et al., 2020; Hori et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: All NORs contain methylated and unmethylated 47S rDNA clusters, and the methylated rDNA repeats within each NOR tend to cluster together to form heterochromatic regions.
source: This study demonstrated that all the NORs contain methylated and unmethylated 47 S rDNA clusters, and the methylated rDNA repeats within each NOR tend to cluster together to form heterochromatic regions (van Sluis et al., 2020; Hori et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: Cis-regulatory elements and factors, including ncRNAs, are suggested to maintain active versus inactive rDNA repeats within each NOR.
source: Cis-regulatory elements and factors, including ncRNAs are suggested to maintain active versus inactive rDNA repeats within each NOR.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on current understanding of rDNA regulation.

claim: The nucleolus harbors a diverse set of small and long noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) that play crucial roles in organizing the nucleolar genome and regulating rRNA expression.
source: The nucleolus harbors a diverse set of small and long noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs), which play crucial roles in organizing the nucleolar genome as well as regulating rRNA expression (Mamontova et al., 2021; Hao and Prasanth, 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: The intergenic spacer (IGS) between rRNA genes encodes several ncRNAs such as pRNA, PAPAS, and PNCTR that modulate rRNA expression and nucleolus organization.
source: For example, the intergenic spacer (IGS) between rRNA genes encodes several ncRNAs, such as pRNA, PAPAS, and PNCTR, which modulate rRNA expression and nucleolus organization (Mamontova et al., 2021; Hao and Prasanth, 2022; Bierhoff et al., 2010; Yap et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: NcRNAs including SLERT, LoNa, AluRNAs, and LETN lncRNAs modulate nucleolus structure and rRNA expression via independent mechanisms.
source: Recent studies have reported that ncRNAs, including SLERT, LoNa, AluRNAs, and the LETN lncRNAs, modulate nucleolus structure and rRNA expression via independent mechanisms (Caudron-Herger et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: NcRNAs play important roles in controlling key nucleolus functions, contributing to cellular homeostasis.
source: Collectively, these studies underscore the importance of ncRNAs in controlling key nucleolus functions, thus contributing to cellular homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective findings of cited studies on nucleolar ncRNAs.

claim: The DNA sequences within the short arms of all five NOR-containing acrocentric chromosomes are highly repetitive and share high levels of sequence similarities across different chromosomes.
source: Besides the rDNA array, the remaining DNA sequences within the short arms of all five NOR-containing acrocentric chromosomes are highly repetitive and share high levels of sequence similarities across different chromosomes (McStay, 2016; Guetg and Santoro, 2012; McStay and Grummt, 2008; Floutsakou et al., 2013; Németh et al., 2010; Németh and Längst, 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from cited previous studies.

claim: Insights into novel genes and/or regulatory elements within the p-arms are limited.
source: As a result, insights into novel genes and/or regulatory elements within the p-arms are limited.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the state of genomic annotation.

claim: Small regions located adjacent to NORs code for lncRNAs.
source: Careful analyses of small regions located adjacent to NORs revealed that they code for lncRNAs (Floutsakou et al., 2013; van Sluis et al., 2019), indicating that the p-arms of the NOR-containing chromosomes harbor ncRNA genes, which could modulate key nucleolar functions.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from cited previous studies.

claim: The p-arms of NOR-containing chromosomes harbor ncRNA genes that could modulate key nucleolar functions.
source: Careful analyses of small regions located adjacent to NORs revealed that they code for lncRNAs (Floutsakou et al., 2013; van Sluis et al., 2019), indicating that the p-arms of the NOR-containing chromosomes harbor ncRNA genes, which could modulate key nucleolar functions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discovery of lncRNAs in p-arm regions.

claim: SNULs likely originate from the p-arms of acrocentric chromosomes.
source: In the present study, we have identified a novel family of ncRNAs: SNULs, which likely originate from the p-arms of acrocentric chromosomes and form allele-specific constrained sub-nucleolar territories on the NOR-containing chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the association of SNULs with NOR-containing chromosomes.

claim: SNULs form allele-specific constrained sub-nucleolar territories on NOR-containing chromosomes.
source: In the present study, we have identified a novel family of ncRNAs: SNULs, which likely originate from the p-arms of acrocentric chromosomes and form allele-specific constrained sub-nucleolar territories on the NOR-containing chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing SNUL association with specific chromosome alleles.

claim: SNUL-1 RNA displays high sequence similarity to pre-rRNA.
source: SNUL-1 RNA displays high sequence similarity to pre-rRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The SNUL family of ncRNAs contributes to rRNA expression.
source: Further studies revealed that the SNUL family of ncRNAs contributes to rRNA expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental data showing altered rRNA levels and processing in SNUL-depleted cells.

claim: SNULs display monoallelic coating/association on the autosomal segments of NOR-containing p-arms for modulating rRNA expression.
source: Thus, our study unraveled the existence of a novel family of ncRNAs that display monoallelic coating/association on the autosomal segments of NOR-containing p-arms for modulating rRNA expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by DNA-RNA-FISH data showing monoallelic SNUL association and functional data showing effects on rRNA expression.
